handsOnLab.brief: You will audit local administrator membership across machines with PowerShell, classify every admin account as legitimate or removable, and draft per-application elevation policies for the five most common elevation requests. The artifact is the pre-rollout report a junior operator delivers before removing local admin.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every admin account is classified with a decision; the five elevation policies are scoped and time-bound; no standing admin remains without a ticketed justification.
handsOnLab.deliverable: elevation-audit.md — admin inventory, per-account decisions, and five per-application elevation policies.
steps: On your test machine, run Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators and record every member: name, object class, and source.

Extend the audit: write a PowerShell loop that reads a list of machine names from machines.txt and runs Invoke-Command to collect each machine's Administrators group — run it against your lab machines.

Classify each account: REMOVE (former employee, vendor account past its need, duplicate), KEEP-TICKETED (break-glass local admin with a sealed password), or REPLACE-WITH-POLICY (daily-use accounts that need specific elevated tasks).
For each REPLACE-WITH-POLICY account, interview-style: list the actual tasks they perform that need elevation (installers, driver updates, specific admin tools).
Draft five per-application elevation policies in a table: Application | Publisher | Scope (users/machines) | Conditions | Duration | Approver | Review date.
Write the helpdesk elevation request workflow as a runbook: intake fields, identity verification step, approval matrix (standard vs sensitive), execution logging, and post-hoc review sampling.
Define the emergency lane: who can approve after hours, what evidence is required, and the mandatory next-business-day review.
Write the rollback criterion for the rollout: what measured signal pauses the local-admin removal (e.g., legitimate elevation requests exceeding capacity).
Document the break-glass account: where the sealed credential lives, who can unseal it, and what alert fires on its use.
Read the finished audit as the auditor from the drill: confirm you can answer 'who had admin last Tuesday' from your logging design.

mockTask.explain: Hit all five points: remove standing admin (why — credential theft pivot), just-in-time per-application elevation, the ticketed/logged workflow, the emergency lane, and the audit answer. That is the complete operator story for this module.
mockTask.q: Panel question: 'Our developers all run as local admins today. How would you take that away without stopping their work?'

notes.body: Local administrator rights are the single most consequential privilege on a Windows endpoint, and their removal is the single highest-leverage hardening step you can take. Understand why before you touch anything. An administrator can install software, modify system configuration, read other users' data, disable security tooling, and — critically — access credential material stored on the machine. When an attacker compromises a standard user, they get that user's files. When they compromise a local admin, they get the machine's credential store: hashes and tokens they can reuse to move laterally, often all the way to domain dominance. This is the pivot: local admin turns a single phished workstation into a stepping stone toward the entire environment. The statistics-free version of the argument is structural, not numerical: every privilege-escalation path, every credential-theft technique, and every persistence mechanism is easier, quieter, or only possible with administrative rights. Removing local admin does not make attacks impossible — it lowers every attack's ceiling and raises its noise. Worked example: two identical phishing compromises. On machine A the user is a local admin. The payload reads credential material from memory, reuses it against the file server, and within the hour the attacker holds a domain-level foothold. On machine B the user is standard. The payload runs in a low-privilege context: it cannot read the credential store, cannot install a driver-level persistence mechanism, cannot disable the agent. Its privilege-escalation attempts — the classic next step — hit the elevation policy and are denied and logged. The same initial click produces a contained single-machine event instead of an enterprise incident. The difference is entirely the standing privilege. Common gotcha: the 'but they need it' reflex. In practice, when organizations audit actual admin usage, the overwhelming majority of daily admin-rights usage is habit, not need: installing approved software (handled by software deployment), changing the clock (handled by policy), running a legacy tool once (handled by an elevation rule). The operator's job is to discover the real needs — which you do in monitor mode — and serve them with scoped elevation rather than standing privilege. Second gotcha: removing admin without the workflow. Take the privilege on Monday with no elevation path and by Wednesday the business has either revolted or routed around you. The removal and the just-in-time workflow ship together, always.  Before removing anything, measure. Pull 30 days of privilege-use data: which users invoke admin rights, for what operations, and how often. You will typically find three groups: the handful with genuine recurring needs (their tasks become elevation rules), the large middle whose 'need' is one legacy installer (their need becomes a scoped rule plus a remediation ticket), and the long tail who simply have admin because everyone does (their need evaporates on inspection). This data does two jobs: it designs the replacement policies, and it defuses the political fight — 'we measured, and here is what you actually use' beats 'trust us' in every meeting where admin removal is contested.
notes.title: Why local admin must go

notes.body: Just-in-time elevation is the replacement for standing admin: instead of the user holding administrative rights all day, the specific application or task is elevated for a scoped, time-bound need — then the privilege is gone. The user account itself never becomes an administrator. This distinction matters enormously. When you make someone a local admin, you grant a standing capability: every process they launch, every script they run, every piece of malware that lands in their session inherits administrative rights until someone remembers to remove them. When you elevate just the installer via policy, only that installer, launched for that task, holds the rights — the user's browser, email client, and everything else stay standard. The policy anatomy has five fields. Identity: which application may be elevated (publisher, hash, or path — the M02 identity discipline applies here too). Scope: which users or groups, on which machines. Conditions: when — business hours, ticket reference required, approval needed above a risk threshold. Duration: how long the elevation lasts — minutes for an installer, never permanent. Logging: every grant records who, what, why, when, and approved-by. Worked example: the monthly vendor driver update. Policy: 'VendorDriverSetup.exe, publisher Vendor Inc., may be elevated for the Helpdesk group on workstation OU, during business hours, with a ticket number, for 30 minutes, approved by the IT lead.' The technician runs the installer through the elevation workflow, it completes with admin rights, the window closes. The technician's account was standard before, during (outside that process), and after. Contrast with the old world: the technician is a local admin all month for a 10-minute task. Common gotcha: elevating the user 'temporarily' instead of the application. 'Temporary admin for the afternoon' is standing admin with a shorter memory — everything in the session inherits it, including the malware. Elevate the task, not the person. Second gotcha: elevation without conditions. An elevation rule with no ticket requirement, no time bound, and no approval is just admin rights with extra steps. The conditions are the control; write them tightly and review them quarterly.  Keep interactive elevation and non-interactive privilege strictly separated in your design. Services and scheduled tasks that run with stored credentials or as SYSTEM are not 'elevation' in the just-in-time sense — they are standing privilege by another name, and they get their own inventory, their own review, and their own hardening (managed service accounts, credential rotation, minimal rights). The just-in-time workflow covers the human asking for temporary rights; the service inventory covers the machine acting with permanent ones. Auditing one while ignoring the other leaves half the privilege surface unexamined.
notes.title: Just-in-time elevation: elevate the task, not the person

notes.body: Elevation policies are written per application, because different software has different legitimate needs and the policy must match the need — no more, no less. Start by categorizing the elevation requests you will actually see. Installers and updaters: the most common legitimate need. Policy: the vendor's signed installer may elevate, scoped to the machines that need the software, time-bound to the deployment window. Management agents: backup, patching, and monitoring tools that genuinely require system-level access. Policy: the agent's service binary is elevated by design (services run as SYSTEM), but its interactive components are not — scope carefully. Administrative utilities: disk tools, driver installers, network diagnostics. Policy: named tools for named groups (IT staff), with ticket requirements for the sensitive ones. Legacy line-of-business apps: the painful category — old software that demands admin for no good reason. Policy: explicit elevation rules as a bridge, paired with a remediation plan (vendor engagement, compatibility shims, or replacement) and a review date, because 'legacy needs admin' cannot be a permanent answer. Worked example: build the policy set for a 25-seat office. The PDF reader's updater: signed updater, may elevate, all workstations, automatic — no ticket needed, it is routine. The accounting package installer: signed installer, may elevate for the IT group only, during the quarterly update window, ticket required. The disk-imaging tool: IT group only, ticket required, 2-hour window, approved by the IT lead. The legacy label-printer driver (unsigned, demands admin): hash-pinned, warehouse machines only, ticket required, 90-day review, vendor contacted about a signed version. Four applications, four different policies, each matching the actual need. Common gotcha: one elevation policy for everything. 'IT staff may elevate anything' recreates standing admin for the highest-value targets — attackers specifically hunt IT credentials. Even IT gets per-application policies, with the sensitive ones requiring approval. Second gotcha: forgetting service accounts and scheduled tasks. Elevation policy covers interactive elevation; services and scheduled tasks with stored credentials are a separate inventory with their own review — a service running as SYSTEM with a weak password is admin rights by another name.  Verify before you elevate. An elevation policy that approves 'the vendor installer' should still confirm the installer's integrity at approval time: compare its hash against the vendor's published value, confirm the signature chains correctly, and confirm you fetched it from the vendor's official distribution point. Elevating a trojaned installer with administrative rights is the worst possible outcome of this control — the policy that grants the privilege must also demand the evidence. Build the verification step into the intake form so it cannot be skipped under time pressure: no hash check, no elevation.
notes.title: Elevation policies per application

notes.body: User Account Control is the prompt everyone loves to hate, and you need to understand exactly what it does and does not do before you layer policy over it. UAC has two prompt types. The consent prompt appears for administrators: 'Do you want to allow this app to make changes?' — a yes/no question to someone who already holds the rights. The credential prompt appears for standard users: 'Enter an administrator username and password' — a demand for credentials the user should not have. UAC's security value is real but narrow: it makes privilege use visible and gives malware one more click to socially engineer. Its weakness is structural: the decision is made by the user, at the moment, under time pressure — which is precisely when users click 'Yes' on whatever the urgent-looking installer demands. Malware has exploited this for years with fake installers that simply ask. Elevation Control moves the decision from the user to the policy. Under policy-driven elevation, the user does not get a yes/no prompt to adjudicate — the agent consults policy: is this application approved for elevation, for this user, under these conditions? If yes, it elevates with full logging. If no, it denies with full logging. The user experience actually improves: legitimate workflows elevate silently per policy instead of interrupting with prompts, while illegitimate ones are denied consistently rather than depending on the user's judgment at 4:55 PM on a Friday. Worked example: the standard-user accountant runs the approved payroll update. Old world: credential prompt, accountant calls helpdesk, helpdesk types the admin password (which the accountant shoulder-surfs), update runs. New world: the payroll updater matches the elevation policy (signed, IT-approved, ticket window), elevates without a prompt, logs the grant. Same outcome, no password shared, full audit trail. Now the attack case: malware drops a fake updater and triggers a UAC consent prompt on an admin's machine — the admin, busy, clicks Yes. Under elevation policy on a standard-user machine, there is no Yes to click: the binary is not in the elevation policy, so it is denied and logged. Common gotcha: thinking UAC 'is' the elevation control. UAC is a speed bump; policy-driven elevation is a gate. Keep UAC enabled (it still catches the unpolicied cases) but never rely on user judgment as the control. Second gotcha: 'quiet mode' UAC settings that auto-elevate. Any setting that removes the prompt without adding policy just removes the speed bump — verify UAC is at a sane level as part of the M08 Defender-plus-baseline work.
notes.title: UAC interplay: prompts are not policy

notes.body: Walk the stolen-credential scenario end to end, because this is the story the panel wants to hear and the threat the control defeats. The setup: a helpdesk technician with local admin on 200 workstations reuses a password. An attacker phishes the technician, harvests the credential, and now holds administrative rights on every machine the technician touched. Under standing admin, the attacker's next moves are textbook: authenticate to workstations with the stolen credential, read credential material from each newly owned machine, escalate toward domain admin, deploy ransomware enterprise-wide. The technician's single credential was a skeleton key because the privilege was standing, broad, and reusable. Now replay with Elevation Control deployed. The technician is a standard user. Their daily elevated tasks — running the approved installer, the driver update — were performed through just-in-time elevation: the task elevated, the account did not. The phished credential is a standard-user credential: it authenticates, but it grants no administrative rights anywhere. The attacker's lateral movement attempts hit closed doors: no admin shares to plunder, no credential store readable, no remote admin tools permitted by Network Control policy. To escalate, the attacker must now defeat the elevation policy itself — requesting elevation for an unapproved binary, which is denied and logged, generating the Detect alert that starts the incident response at the attempt stage. The blast radius collapses from 'the enterprise' to 'one standard-user session.' Worked example with the workflow: the attacker, holding the phished standard credential, submits an elevation request for their payload through the helpdesk channel (the only path). Identity verification fails — the requester cannot prove they are the technician under duress procedures — and even a social-engineered approval would only elevate the named application for a time-bound window, not the attacker's session. Every step is logged. Common gotcha: believing elevation control replaces credential hygiene. It does not — the phished credential still grants the user's data and email. What it does is cap the damage: credential theft without standing privilege is a contained incident, not an enterprise one. Pair it with phishing-resistant authentication and the attacker's path narrows to nearly nothing. Second gotcha: the break-glass account. You will keep one sealed emergency admin credential — and its use must fire an immediate alert, because in a no-standing-admin world, any use of it is an exceptional event worth waking someone for.  Assume the attacker also steals session tokens, not just passwords — tokens can be replayed without the password ever being known. This is why the control pairs with session hygiene: short token lifetimes, and elevation decisions that re-verify rather than trusting an existing session blindly. The principle is the same as everywhere in this course: standing artifacts — passwords, tokens, privileges — are what attackers reuse. Shrink what stands, time-bound what is granted, and log every grant so the reuse window is visible.
notes.title: The stolen-credential pivot scenario

notes.body: The helpdesk elevation workflow is where policy meets humans, and its design decides whether the control survives. It has five steps, each non-optional. Intake: the requester submits who they are, what application needs elevation, the business reason, the ticket number, and the time window. 'Need admin plz' is not an intake — the form enforces the evidence. Identity verification: the helpdesk verifies the requester is who they claim — callback to the known number, in-person for sensitive requests, never trust the request channel alone (the 'urgent admin request' email from the 'CFO' is a classic social-engineering lure). Scoped approval: the approver checks the application against policy — is this app approved for elevation for this user? If yes and routine, approve; if sensitive or unprecedented, escalate to the security lead. The approval names the application, the machine, and the window — never 'admin for the afternoon.' Execution with logging: the elevation is granted through the agent, and the grant is logged with who, what, why, window, and approver. Post-hoc review: a sample of grants is reviewed weekly — was the business reason real, did the window match the need, any anomalies? Worked example: Tuesday 10 AM, a designer needs to install a font management tool. Intake: designer, FontTool Setup 4.2, vendor-signed, ticket HD-4821, today 10-12. Verification: helpdesk calls the designer's known extension. Approval: the tool is on the approved-elevation list for the design group — approved, 2-hour window, this machine. Execution: the installer elevates, completes, window closes. Review: Friday's sample includes HD-4821 — business reason confirmed, window matched. Total friction: one form and one callback. The emergency lane handles the 2 AM server case: on-call approver, same evidence, mandatory next-business-day review — emergencies get speed, not exemption. Common gotcha: verification theater. 'We verified identity' by replying to the same email thread that made the request proves nothing. Verify through an independent channel, every time, especially for sensitive elevations. Second gotcha: approval without expiry. An approved elevation that stays open 'until the work is done' is standing admin with paperwork. The window closes automatically; a new window needs a new approval.  Design the emergency lane with the same care as the standard path, because emergencies are when discipline is weakest. The lane needs three things: a reachable approver (the on-call rotation, not 'whoever is awake'), the same evidence minimum (ticket number, application identity, window — no evidence-free elevations, ever), and a mandatory next-business-day review where the grant is re-examined with cool heads. Publish the lane's usage statistics monthly: a lane used twice a quarter is healthy; a lane used twice a week is a standard path avoiding scrutiny, and the review will show it.
notes.title: The helpdesk elevation request workflow

summary: Local admin is the pivot that turns one phished workstation into an enterprise incident. This module covers its removal and replacement: just-in-time elevation per application, per-application elevation policies, UAC interplay, the stolen-credential scenario that shows what no-standing-admin buys you, and the helpdesk workflow that keeps the business moving.
